case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court’s final merits judgment between completely diverse parties must be vacated after an appellate court later holds that removal was improper because the district court erroneously dismissed the sole nondiverse defendant at the time of removal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332 (diversity jurisdiction), 1441 (removal), 1447(c) (remand for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction/defect), and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure governing interlocutory orders and final judgment (esp. Rule 54(b))—as applied through the final-judgment/merger doctrine and Article III limits on subject-matter jurisdiction.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Hain Celestial and Whole Foods) argue that once the nondiverse party was dismissed and the case proceeded to a final federal judgment solely among completely diverse parties, the federal court’s judgment should not be automatically vacated on appeal merely because the dismissal (which created complete diversity) is later found to have been erroneous. They contend the Fifth Circuit’s rule wastes judicial resources, undermines finality, and encourages post-judgment ‘vertical forum shopping’ (seeking a second merits adjudication in state court after losing in federal court). Petitioners and supporting amici emphasize that final judgments—particularly those turning on case-dispositive rulings like admissibility of scientific expert testimony—should not be wiped out when the parties remaining at judgment were within federal diversity jurisdiction, and they urge a rule that preserves final judgments or otherwise limits vacatur/remand to the jurisdictional defect actually present at the time judgment was entered.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Palmquists) argue that the district court never had proper removal jurisdiction because the sole nondiverse defendant was wrongly dismissed at the time of removal, meaning the federal court should not have proceeded at all. Because that dismissal order was interlocutory and remained revisable until it merged into the final judgment, the appellate court’s later correction of the erroneous dismissal necessarily collapses the jurisdictional basis for everything that followed, requiring vacatur of the final judgment and remand. Respondents and supporting amici contend that jurisdiction is assessed based on the true party alignment/joinder at the time removal was invoked, that an erroneous interlocutory dismissal cannot ‘manufacture’ removal jurisdiction, and that preserving the federal judgment would improperly validate an ultra vires exercise of federal judicial power and dilute statutory limits Congress placed on removal.
key_precedents: DiCenzo v. A-Best Prods. Co., 897 N.E.2d 132 (Ohio 2008)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point: Caterpillar’s focus on diversity at the moment of final judgment and the institutional costs of making jurisdiction turn on later merits reversals. But Caterpillar presupposed a lawful, stable cure before judgment; as Justice Alito emphasizes, an interlocutory dismissal later held erroneous never validly eliminated the nondiverse party, and under Rule 54(b)/merger the final judgment cannot be insulated by a party lineup that existed only by reversible error. Justice Thomas’s “jurisdiction-at-judgment” principle has force, yet it assumes the judgment rests on a configuration properly before the court; otherwise we invite jurisdiction by mistake, effectively expanding §§ 1332 and 1441 contrary to § 1447(c)’s remand command when the defect is revealed. A narrow holding distinguishing Caterpillar on the ground that the only purported cure was legally ineffective best preserves both precedent and statutory limits without creating a broad retroactivity rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito offer the strongest respondent point: that an interlocutory dismissal later reversed “merges” into the final judgment, so the nondiverse party was never properly out and diversity never properly existed. But merger and Rule 54(b) are judge-made appellate-review doctrines; they cannot supply a retroactive, jurisdiction-destroying “relation back” rule absent in the text of § 1332, § 1441, or § 1447(c), and § 1447(c) speaks to remand while the case is pending, not mandatory post-judgment nullification. Caterpillar’s removal-specific rule draws the relevant statutory line at whether complete diversity existed when final judgment was entered in the case as then constituted, and nothing in Grupo Dataflux (a time-of-filing/citizenship-change case) compels treating later merits reversal as proving a lack of jurisdiction at judgment. Accepting respondent’s merger-based reconstruction would make federal jurisdiction turn on subsequent merits corrections rather than on Congress’s enacted jurisdictional requirements at the time the court exercised power.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is their Caterpillar “jurisdiction at judgment” rule and the fear that appellate merits reversals will make jurisdiction unstable. But Caterpillar assumed a legally effective cure before judgment; here, as the Chief Justice stresses, the only “cure” was an interlocutory dismissal later held erroneous, which under Rule 54(b) and ordinary merger principles means the nondiverse defendant was never properly out for § 1332/§ 1441 purposes. Treating a reversible, ultra vires dismissal as jurisdiction-creating would let district courts manufacture removal jurisdiction by error, in tension with § 1447(c)’s command to remand when jurisdiction is lacking and with Grupo Dataflux’s warning against post hoc validation of judgments entered without true jurisdiction. Finality concerns cannot override Congress’s limits on removal, and the remedy here is vacatur and remand rather than insulating the federal judgment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point: Caterpillar’s finality-driven focus on diversity as of final judgment, and the concern that merger doctrine would make jurisdiction hinge on later merits reversals. But Caterpillar assumed a legally effective, stable cure (there, a proper elimination of the nondiverse party), whereas here—per Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito—the only route to “diversity at judgment” was an interlocutory dismissal that lacked Rule 54(b) finality and was later held erroneous, so treating it as jurisdiction-conferring would let reversible error manufacture removal power beyond §§ 1441 and 1332. I also do not read § 1447(c)’s remand instruction as evaporating post-judgment when the court of appeals’ correction shows the case was never within the statutory grant as properly understood; that pragmatic reading protects plaintiffs from strategic removals and preserves access to a proper forum. Grupo Dataflux reinforces the principle that finality cannot validate judgments where jurisdiction depends on an improper party configuration, and it counsels against expanding federal jurisdiction through post hoc rationalizations.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s merger/retroactivity point is the strongest respondent argument: that reversal of an interlocutory dismissal means the nondiverse party was never properly out, so diversity was never lawfully present. But merger and Rule 54(b) are judge-made appellate-review doctrines, and—under Caterpillar’s pragmatic reading of the removal scheme—they do not supply a textual basis in § 1332 or § 1447(c) to retroactively nullify a final judgment when the parties before the district court at judgment were completely diverse. Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of Grupo Dataflux usefully polices "manufactured" jurisdiction, yet Dataflux is a time-of-filing/citizenship-change case and does not establish that a later merits reversal converts an otherwise diverse, final-judgment posture into a statutory jurisdictional defect. I therefore remain persuaded that § 1447(c) is best read as a pre-judgment remand directive, and that importing merger to mandate post-judgment vacatur would reintroduce the waste-and-finality problem Caterpillar sought to avoid absent clear statutory command.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s merger/Rule 54(b) argument is the best respondent point, but it asks us to let judge-made appellate finality doctrines do work Congress did not assign them—retroactively altering the § 1332 party lineup and converting a completed judgment into a jurisdictional nullity. Caterpillar’s logic is that once complete diversity exists when judgment is entered, the remaining problem is an antecedent removal defect remediable by timely remand under § 1447(c), not automatic post-judgment vacatur absent clear statutory text; importing merger doctrine would make jurisdiction depend on later merits reversals, precisely the instability Caterpillar sought to avoid. Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of Grupo Dataflux usefully cautions against manufacturing jurisdiction, but Dataflux addresses jurisdiction that never existed at judgment (time-of-filing/citizenship problems), whereas here the district court had diversity jurisdiction as the case then stood and only later merits correction would “undo” the dismissal. Under a textualist/originalist approach, neither § 1332 nor § 1447(c) clearly commands the wasteful remedy respondents seek, so I remain with petitioner.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch offer the strongest pushback by reading Caterpillar to make diversity at the moment of final judgment dispositive and warning against letting later merits reversals unsettle jurisdiction. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito explain, Caterpillar assumed a legally effective, stable cure (a proper elimination of the nondiverse party) before judgment; here the only “cure” was an interlocutory dismissal later held erroneous, which under Rule 54(b) and the merger principle means the nondiverse party was never lawfully out of the case for purposes of Congress’s § 1332/§ 1441 limits. Treating a reversible merits error as sufficient to “manufacture” diversity would undermine § 1447(c)’s remand command and invite strategic removals premised on district-court mistakes—an institutional cost Caterpillar did not endorse. Grupo Dataflux reinforces the broader caution that finality cannot validate a merits judgment when the jurisdictional defect, properly understood, persists through judgment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s merger/retroactivity argument is the strongest respondent point, but I do not see in the text of § 1332, § 1441, or § 1447(c) any directive that a later appellate reversal of an interlocutory dismissal “relates back” to negate subject-matter jurisdiction that indisputably existed on the face of the party lineup when final judgment was entered. Merger and Rule 54(b), as Justice Gorsuch notes, are judge-made doctrines about appellate review and finality; using them to reconstruct the party configuration for jurisdictional purposes risks making statutory jurisdiction turn on later merits corrections rather than the court’s power at the time it acted. Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Grupo Dataflux usefully cautions against finality saving a judgment where the jurisdictional defect persisted through judgment, but here diversity did not persist as a defect at judgment—only the antecedent removal error remained, which Caterpillar treats as remediable via timely remand rather than post-judgment nullification absent a clear statutory command. On an originalist/textualist account, respondent’s rule would add a jurisdiction-destroying “merger” gloss to the statutes that Congress did not enact.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s merger-doctrine framing is the most serious respondent point, because it tries to recast the later appellate reversal as proving diversity never lawfully existed. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, neither § 1332 nor § 1447(c) incorporates merger or Rule 54(b) “relation back” concepts as a jurisdictional test, and Caterpillar’s pragmatic focus is whether the district court had diversity power to enter the final judgment in the case as it then stood on the docket. Justice Alito’s reliance on Grupo Dataflux sharpens the concern about manufacturing jurisdiction, but Dataflux addresses post-filing citizenship changes in original jurisdiction and does not supply a clear statutory command to unwind a completed removal judgment solely because an interlocutory merits dismissal is later corrected. On procedural-fairness and consequences grounds, I remain unpersuaded that we should create a post-judgment vacatur rule that turns federal jurisdiction on later merits reversals absent unmistakable direction from Congress.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1447(c) requires remand when subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking, and here the case was not properly removable because complete diversity did not exist at removal once the erroneously dismissed nondiverse defendant is restored on appeal. Because that dismissal was interlocutory (absent a Rule 54(b) final judgment) and merged into the final judgment, correcting it on appeal means the district court lacked Article III/statutory diversity jurisdiction throughout, so the ensuing merits judgment cannot stand. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis allows a final judgment to stand only when the jurisdictional defect is genuinely cured before judgment; an erroneous interlocutory dismissal that is later reversed does not supply the kind of stable cure Caterpillar relied on. Preserving the judgment would undermine Congress’s removal limits in §§ 1441 and 1447(c) and invite post hoc validation of ultra vires federal adjudication, contrary to institutional legitimacy and settled jurisdictional principles.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The relevant jurisdictional text is 28 U.S.C. § 1332, which requires complete diversity at the time the federal court enters final judgment; here, once the nondiverse defendant had been dismissed and the final merits judgment was entered between completely diverse parties, Article III and § 1332 were satisfied at that critical time. Any error in removal under §§ 1441 and 1447(c) was a statutory defect at the time of removal, not a continuing absence of subject-matter jurisdiction at judgment, and the statutes do not compel vacatur of an otherwise valid final judgment when jurisdiction exists at judgment. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis holds that where diversity jurisdiction exists at the time of final judgment, considerations of finality and the limits of § 1447(c) do not require undoing a completed federal adjudication merely because removal was improper when taken. An appellate conclusion that the interlocutory dismissal was erroneous does not retroactively negate the district court’s power to render judgment among diverse parties once that was the case.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1332 require complete diversity as a jurisdictional predicate, and an erroneous interlocutory dismissal of the sole nondiverse defendant at the time of removal cannot manufacture jurisdiction that never properly existed under §§ 1441 and 1447(c). Under the final-judgment/merger doctrine and Rule 54(b), the interlocutory dismissal merges into the final judgment, so correcting that error on appeal restores the nondiverse party’s presence and defeats diversity, requiring vacatur because the court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction to enter final merits judgment. Caterpillar permits affirmance only where the jurisdictional defect has been cured so that federal jurisdiction exists at the time of judgment; here, once the dismissal is deemed erroneous, the defect is not cured at judgment. Grupo Dataflux confirms that considerations of finality and efficiency do not justify sustaining a judgment entered without subject-matter jurisdiction and limits Caterpillar to cases with jurisdiction at the time of final judgment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Removal jurisdiction must be proper at the time it is invoked, and an erroneous interlocutory dismissal of the sole nondiverse defendant cannot "manufacture" diversity jurisdiction that Congress withheld under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332 and 1441. Because the dismissal order remained revisable and merged into the final judgment under the final-judgment/merger doctrine (and Rule 54(b) principles), correcting that error on appeal restores the true party configuration and reveals a lack of removal jurisdiction requiring remand under 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c). Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis permits affirmance only when the jurisdictional defect has been cured before final judgment; here, the defect persisted because diversity existed at judgment only due to the very interlocutory error the court of appeals properly corrected, so finality concerns cannot justify validating an ultra vires exercise of federal power. This approach protects fairness and access to justice by ensuring plaintiffs are not forced into federal court through mistaken dismissals that strip them of their chosen state forum and potentially disadvantage vulnerable litigants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), an improper removal does not compel vacatur where complete diversity exists by the time of final judgment and the remaining flaw is the statutory removal defect at the outset, because finality and judicial economy weigh strongly against unwinding a fully litigated merits judgment. Here, once the nondiverse defendant had been dismissed and the final judgment ran only between completely diverse parties, the district court had subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332 at the critical time for Article III power (final judgment), even if removal under § 1441 was erroneous when taken. While 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c) requires remand when subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking, Caterpillar’s workable compromise recognizes that a cured diversity defect should not automatically trigger vacatur after a full federal adjudication. Treating the interlocutory dismissal’s later reversal as retroactively invalidating jurisdiction would elevate a correctable pre-judgment defect over the statute’s and system’s interests in finality, workability, and coherent administration of diversity jurisdiction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III and 28 U.S.C. § 1332 require complete diversity at the time judgment is entered, and where the case as it stood at final judgment involved only completely diverse parties, the district court possessed subject-matter jurisdiction to enter that judgment. Section 1447(c) speaks to remand when a case “was removed improvidently” or when jurisdiction is lacking, but it does not compel automatic vacatur of a merits judgment when the jurisdictional defect existing at removal has been cured before final judgment. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis holds that an initially improper removal does not require disturbing a final judgment once complete diversity exists at judgment, emphasizing finality and the limited remedial role of appellate courts when Article III jurisdiction is present at the end of the case. Treating an interlocutory dismissal later deemed erroneous as retroactively nullifying an otherwise jurisdictionally proper final judgment would elevate procedural missteps over Congress’s jurisdictional line as written and invite wasteful relitigation without a clear statutory command.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III and Congress’s removal limits in 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332, 1441, and 1447(c) require that federal courts possess subject-matter jurisdiction at the time they enter final judgment; if the only basis for diversity jurisdiction was an interlocutory dismissal later held erroneous, the district court ultimately lacked power to render a merits judgment and the proper remedy is vacatur. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis permits a final judgment to stand only when the jurisdictional defect has been cured before judgment (there, by a voluntary settlement and dismissal of the nondiverse party), not when the “cure” was itself legally invalid. Royal Canin U.S.A., Inc. v. Wullschleger underscores that when jurisdiction is absent at the time of judgment, vacatur (not pragmatism) is required, and preserving such a judgment would effectively validate an ultra vires exercise of federal jurisdiction. While efficiency and finality matter, they cannot override statutory and constitutional jurisdictional limits, and the merger doctrine confirms that the erroneous dismissal infects the final judgment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1332, the relevant Article III question is whether complete diversity existed when the district court entered final judgment; if it did, the court possessed subject-matter jurisdiction at that critical point. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), teaches that an erroneous removal need not require vacatur when the jurisdictional defect (lack of complete diversity) is cured before judgment, because finality, efficiency, and economy outweigh undoing a fully litigated merits judgment where federal jurisdiction existed at judgment. Although § 1447(c) directs remand when removal is improper, its remedial command cannot override the presence of subject-matter jurisdiction at the time of judgment, and precedent counsels preserving final judgments absent a jurisdictional defect that persisted through judgment. The erroneous interlocutory dismissal of the nondiverse defendant may have been reversible error on the merits, but it should not retroactively nullify a final judgment entered in a case that, as it then stood, satisfied § 1332.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I would reverse, because where complete diversity indisputably existed at the time of final judgment, Article III subject-matter jurisdiction was present, and the remaining problem is an antecedent statutory removal error under 28 U.S.C. § 1441/§ 1447(c) rather than a continuing jurisdictional defect. Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), once a diversity case has proceeded to final judgment with complete diversity, considerations of finality, efficiency, and economy strongly counsel against automatic vacatur for an initial removal defect that was cured before judgment. Treating the earlier interlocutory dismissal error as necessarily requiring wholesale vacatur would invite wasteful relitigation and strategic post-judgment attempts to obtain a second merits adjudication in state court, undermining practical consequences and procedural fairness. The proper remedy should be tailored to defects existing at the time of judgment; if jurisdiction existed then, the federal merits judgment should generally stand notwithstanding the earlier removal irregularity.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court’s final judgment between completely diverse parties must be vacated after an appellate court later concludes that removal was improper because the district court wrongly dismissed the only nondiverse defendant at the removal stage.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1332 (diversity jurisdiction); 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441, 1446, and 1447 (removal and remand framework), especially § 1447(c) (mandatory remand for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction); plus the federal final-judgment/merger principle and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b) (interlocutory orders subject to revision until final judgment).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that once the case proceeded in federal court to a final judgment resolving claims among parties who are completely diverse, that final judgment should not be undone merely because a nondiverse party was erroneously dismissed earlier at removal. They contend the Fifth Circuit’s rule forces vacatur and a full do-over in state court even where the ultimate judgment involved only diverse parties, undermining finality, wasting judicial resources, and encouraging post-judgment ‘vertical forum shopping’ (seeking a second bite in state court after losing in federal court). Petitioners and supporting amici emphasize practical harms in complex litigation (including product-liability cases involving dispositive expert-evidence rulings) and urge a rule that preserves final judgments where, at the time judgment is entered, the jurisdictional defect has been cured or is no longer outcome-determinative as to the judgment between diverse parties.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that because the district court’s dismissal of the sole nondiverse party at the time of removal was erroneous and remained interlocutory (and revisable) until it merged into the final judgment, the federal court lacked proper removal jurisdiction to proceed to final judgment, and the judgment must be vacated. They maintain that the statutory removal scheme (especially § 1447(c)) requires remand when subject-matter jurisdiction is absent, and that a defendant should not be able to manufacture federal jurisdiction through an erroneous dismissal at removal and then claim finality to insulate that error. Respondents and supporting amici (including civil procedure professors and AAJ) frame the Fifth Circuit’s approach as consistent with jurisdiction-first principles and with the idea that final judgments cannot stand when the case was improperly in federal court due to lack of complete diversity at the critical jurisdictional moment.
key_precedents: DiCenzo v. A-Best Prods. Co., 897 N.E.2d 132 (Ohio 2008)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “manufactured jurisdiction” point is the hardest one, but it still treats an interlocutory merits error as if it were an enduring subject-matter jurisdiction defect; under Caterpillar the dispositive question, post-judgment, is whether complete diversity existed when final judgment entered. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, importing merger/Rule 54(b) into § 1447(c) would turn any arguably erroneous interlocutory ruling affecting party composition into a jurisdictional time bomb, forcing automatic vacatur untethered to any lack of § 1332 jurisdiction at judgment. Grupo Dataflux, which Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas highlight, limits cure-by-postfiling changes in original-jurisdiction cases but preserves Caterpillar’s removal-specific finality rule where the defect is cured before judgment; that boundary answers the worry about expanding Caterpillar too far. A narrow holding—preserving the final judgment because diversity existed at entry, while making clear we do not bless strategic manipulation and that the dismissal error remains reviewable on ordinary appellate grounds—best protects finality and the Court’s institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “manufactured jurisdiction” argument, grounded in merger and Rule 54(b) revisability, is the most serious challenge, but it does not identify any statutory text making an earlier interlocutory error a continuing jurisdictional defect once complete diversity exists at the time of final judgment. As Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice emphasize, § 1447(c) directs remand when the court “lacks subject matter jurisdiction,” and by the time judgment was entered the case (as then constituted) satisfied Article III and § 1332, so the statute does not compel post-judgment vacatur. Grupo Dataflux, as Justice Kagan notes, cabins cure-by-postfiling changes in original-jurisdiction cases but preserves Caterpillar’s removal-specific rule that a cured defect before judgment does not require undoing a fully litigated merits judgment. Under an originalist, textualist approach, we should not convert merger doctrine into an atextual mandate to nullify final judgments despite undisputed jurisdiction at the decisive moment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “manufactured jurisdiction” objection—rooted in merger and Rule 54(b)’s revisability—is the best argument for respondent, but it still conflates an antecedent merits error with the statutory question whether the court “lacks subject-matter jurisdiction” when it enters final judgment under § 1447(c). As the Chief Justice notes, Caterpillar draws an administrable, consequences-sensitive line at final judgment: if complete diversity exists then, the federal court is not acting without § 1332 jurisdiction in the posture in which it renders judgment, even if an interlocutory dismissal that helped create diversity is later deemed wrong. Justice Kagan’s invocation of Grupo Dataflux reinforces the limiting principle rather than undermining Caterpillar: we are strict where the jurisdictional defect persists through judgment, but we do not impose automatic vacatur where the defect is cured before judgment in the removal context. The dismissal’s correctness remains reviewable on appeal (merger), but treating that error as jurisdiction-destroying would create an atextual do-over rule that needlessly sacrifices finality and judicial economy.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press an administrable Caterpillar line keyed to diversity at final judgment, but that framing abstracts away the removal statute’s core safeguard: § 1447(c) makes remand mandatory when jurisdiction is lacking, and here the only “cure” was the district court’s own erroneous, revisable interlocutory dismissal of the nondiverse defendant—a pathway that effectively lets the federal court create the very jurisdiction it initially lacked. Grupo Dataflux, though discussed as a limit on Caterpillar, reinforces my concern that we should not extend Caterpillar to scenarios where the jurisdictional defect is eliminated only by a mistaken merits-adjacent ruling that deprives the plaintiff of the chosen state forum. Justice Kagan’s worry about “time bombs” from interlocutory error is real, but my approach is narrower: it targets only cases where the federal court’s wrong decision about who remains in the suit is the curative mechanism for improper removal, a context where fairness and deterrence of jurisdiction-by-error outweigh post-judgment efficiency. The dismissal error’s appealability (as Justice Roberts notes) does not answer the threshold problem that the federal forum was retained precisely because of that error, so vacatur and remand remain the proper remedy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “manufactured jurisdiction” point is the hardest: if the only curative event is the district court’s own erroneous dismissal, it feels like jurisdiction is being created by mistake. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Caterpillar draws an administrable, text-tethered line at whether the court “lacks subject-matter jurisdiction” when it enters final judgment; once complete diversity exists then, § 1447(c) no longer describes the case’s posture, even if an interlocutory ruling helped get there. Grupo Dataflux, as I noted earlier and Justice Thomas echoes, limits cure-by-postfiling events in original-jurisdiction settings, but it preserves Caterpillar’s removal-specific finality logic and does not convert every antecedent error (reviewable on appeal under merger/Rule 54(b)) into a continuing jurisdictional defect. Treating revisable interlocutory mistakes as jurisdiction-destroying would make final judgments hostage to collateral disputes about the correctness of earlier party-status rulings—an atextual and unworkable expansion of § 1447(c).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “manufactured jurisdiction” argument is serious, but it treats merger and Rule 54(b) revisability as if they retroactively negate subject-matter jurisdiction at the time of final judgment; those doctrines speak to appellate reviewability, not to whether Article III and § 1332 were satisfied when judgment was entered. As the Chief Justice stresses, Caterpillar draws an administrable, text-respecting line at final judgment, and § 1447(c) by its terms commands remand only when the district court “lacks subject-matter jurisdiction,” which it did not once complete diversity existed at judgment. Justice Kagan’s observation about Grupo Dataflux helps confirm the boundary: it limits cure-by-postfiling changes in original-jurisdiction cases but does not displace Caterpillar’s removal-context rule where the defect is cured before judgment. The alleged error in dismissing the nondiverse defendant may be reversible on the merits, but nothing in the removal statutes makes that interlocutory mistake a jurisdictional time bomb that mandates vacatur after a jurisdictionally proper final judgment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “manufactured jurisdiction” point is serious, but I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Caterpillar’s administrable rule hinges on whether complete diversity exists at the time of final judgment, not whether every interlocutory step that produced that posture was error-free. The merger/Rule 54(b) revisability concern identifies why the dismissal can be reviewed on appeal, but it does not convert a past removal mistake into a continuing absence of subject-matter jurisdiction once § 1332 is satisfied at judgment, as Justice Kagan emphasizes. Grupo Dataflux (which Justice Kagan and others invoke) reinforces the boundary: if nondiversity persists through judgment, vacatur is required; where the defect is cured before judgment in the removal context, Caterpillar counsels preserving finality and channeling any error into merits review rather than jurisdictional nullification.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “manufactured jurisdiction” argument—grounded in merger and Rule 54(b) revisability—is the most serious objection, but it conflates an antecedent merits error with the distinct statutory question whether the district court “lacks subject matter jurisdiction” when it enters judgment. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, Caterpillar draws an administrable, text-sensitive line: once complete diversity exists at final judgment, § 1332 is satisfied and § 1447(c)’s remand command is no longer triggered, even if the path to that posture included an erroneous interlocutory dismissal. Grupo Dataflux, which Justice Kagan notes as a limit, reinforces rather than undermines this: it polices cases where nondiversity persists through judgment, but it does not convert every potentially reversible interlocutory party-dismissal into a jurisdictional nullity requiring automatic vacatur after full merits litigation. The proper remedy for an erroneous dismissal remains ordinary appellate review on the merits; treating merger as jurisdiction-destroying would add an atextual, mandatory do-over rule that neither § 1332 nor § 1447(c) supports.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “manufactured jurisdiction” point is serious, but I don’t think it converts an antecedent merits error into a continuing absence of subject-matter jurisdiction once complete diversity indisputably exists at the time of final judgment. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, making the validity of every interlocutory party-dismissal the determinant of post-judgment jurisdiction would destabilize finality and turn Caterpillar’s administrable line into a fact-bound inquiry about whether the cure was “lawful” enough, a standard the removal statutes do not articulate. Rule 54(b) revisability and merger (Sotomayor’s focus) go to whether the dismissal can be corrected on appeal, not to whether § 1332 is satisfied in the case as finally adjudicated; the proper remedy for an erroneous dismissal is appellate reversal, not automatic jurisdictional nullification of an otherwise jurisdictionally proper judgment. Grupo Dataflux cautions against expanding cure doctrines where nondiversity persists through judgment, but here—consistent with the Chief Justice’s framing—the defect is gone by judgment, so vacatur would impose disproportionate, wasteful relitigation without vindicating any ongoing Article III or statutory limit.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), an erroneous failure to remand after improper removal does not require vacatur if Article III and § 1332 diversity requirements are satisfied at the time final judgment is entered; that narrow rule protects finality and conserves judicial resources. Here, once the only nondiverse defendant was dismissed and the case proceeded to a final judgment solely between completely diverse parties, the jurisdictional prerequisites existed at the critical time for judgment, making § 1447(c)’s remand directive inapplicable at the post-judgment stage. Treating the earlier dismissal as an interlocutory error that automatically taints the final judgment would expand § 1447(c) beyond its role and invite wasteful do-overs inconsistent with institutional legitimacy. A limited holding preserving the final judgment while leaving ordinary review of the erroneous dismissal available best fits precedent and the statutory scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The removal statutes require remand when subject-matter jurisdiction is absent, see 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c), but the relevant question here is whether a final judgment must be vacated when complete diversity indisputably existed at the time judgment was entered. Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), an error in denying remand at the outset does not compel undoing a final judgment when the jurisdictional defect has been cured before final judgment and the district court had § 1332 jurisdiction over the case in the posture in which it was finally adjudicated. The Fifth Circuit’s mandatory-vacatur rule elevates an earlier interlocutory misstep (revisable under Rule 54(b) until final judgment) over Article III and § 1332’s core requirement at judgment, and it needlessly disregards finality and judicial economy where the federal court ultimately possessed jurisdiction. Consistent with Caterpillar’s holding and rationale, the final judgment between completely diverse parties should stand notwithstanding an earlier improper removal.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1447(c) mandates remand when the district court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, but where complete diversity exists at the time of final judgment, the remaining flaw is a statutory defect in removal timing rather than a continuing Article III or § 1332 jurisdictional absence. Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), once the jurisdictional defect is cured before judgment, "considerations of finality, efficiency, and economy" counsel against vacatur of a fully litigated federal judgment. Treating an interlocutory dismissal error at removal as automatically requiring post-judgment vacatur invites wasteful do-overs and encourages losing parties to seek a second bite in state court, contrary to the practical-consequences focus of the removal framework. The better rule is to preserve the final judgment where, at the time judgment is entered, the parties are completely diverse and the federal court has § 1332 jurisdiction over the case as it then stands.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1447(c) makes remand mandatory when subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking, and here removal was improper because complete diversity did not exist at the critical removal moment once the district court erroneously dismissed the sole nondiverse defendant. Unlike Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), where the jurisdictional defect was cured before final judgment by a voluntary dismissal/settlement, the defect here was “cured” only by the district court’s own mistaken, interlocutory dismissal that merged into final judgment under the merger principle and remained revisable under Rule 54(b). Allowing a final federal judgment to stand in these circumstances would effectively let an erroneous merits-like ruling at the threshold manufacture federal jurisdiction contrary to the strict limits of § 1332 and the removal statutes. The better course—especially to protect plaintiffs’ chosen state forum and ensure fair access to justice—is to vacate and remand when federal jurisdiction was never properly established through a lawful pathway.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1447(c) mandates remand when subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking, but Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), holds that an erroneous failure to remand at removal does not require vacatur of a final federal judgment if complete diversity exists by the time judgment is entered. Here, once the only nondiverse defendant was out of the case by the time final judgment was rendered, the judgment rests on a proper § 1332 jurisdictional footing, and undoing it would elevate a procedural removal mistake over finality and workability. Grupo Dataflux, 541 U.S. 567 (2004), limits Caterpillar’s rationale but preserves its core holding where the jurisdictional defect is cured before judgment; that is the administrable line consistent with Rule 54(b)’s treatment of interlocutory orders and with the removal statutes’ overall coherence. A contrary rule would systematically incentivize post-judgment relitigation in state court without advancing any substantive jurisdictional interest once § 1332 is satisfied at judgment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The removal statutes make remand mandatory only when the federal court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c), and by the time final judgment entered here the remaining parties were completely diverse under § 1332. Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, an initial removal defect based on incomplete diversity does not require vacatur where complete diversity exists at the time of judgment, because Article III and § 1332 are satisfied when the judgment is entered and the final judgment should not be undone for a cured jurisdictional defect. Treating the earlier erroneous dismissal as automatically infecting the final judgment elevates an interlocutory, revisable ruling (cf. Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b)’s merger principle) over the statutory jurisdictional inquiry at judgment and invites wasteful do-overs contrary to Congress’s calibrated removal framework. Nothing in the plain text of §§ 1441–1447 commands vacatur of a final merits judgment when the only jurisdictional defect no longer exists at the time of judgment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, an erroneous removal based on incomplete diversity at the time of removal does not require undoing a federal judgment when, by the time of final judgment, the parties to that judgment are completely diverse and no jurisdictional defect remains. Reading 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c) to mandate post-judgment vacatur here would elevate an earlier, interlocutory removal error into a rule that defeats finality and imposes substantial practical costs, even though Article III and § 1332 are satisfied at the dispositive moment. Consistent with institutional concerns and workable administration, the better rule is to preserve final judgments where the nondiverse party is not a party to the final judgment, while policing improper removal through timely remand review rather than a mandatory do-over after full merits litigation. This approach respects precedent and the final-judgment/merger principles without inviting defendants to “manufacture” jurisdiction, because jurisdiction must exist at final judgment and any remaining nondiverse party at that point would still require vacatur under cases like Grupo Dataflux.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The removal statutes require remand when subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking, see 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c), but the relevant question here is whether a final judgment must be vacated when complete diversity indisputably existed at the time judgment was entered under 28 U.S.C. § 1332. Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, even though the district court erred in refusing to remand at the outset, a final judgment need not be disturbed if the jurisdictional defect (lack of complete diversity) was cured before final judgment, because considerations of finality, efficiency, and economy become decisive once the case has been fully litigated in federal court. The respondents’ merger/Rule 54(b) theory does not overcome Caterpillar’s core holding that a cured diversity defect does not require post-judgment vacatur, and it would elevate procedural error at removal into an automatic undoing of an otherwise jurisdictionally valid final judgment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), an erroneous failure to remand after improper removal does not require vacatur of a final judgment if the federal jurisdictional requirements (complete diversity under 28 U.S.C. § 1332) are satisfied at the time judgment is entered, because finality, efficiency, and economy become “overwhelming” once the case has been fully litigated in federal court. Here, once the only nondiverse defendant was dismissed and the final judgment resolved claims solely between completely diverse parties, the core Article III/§ 1332 concern—adjudication without subject-matter jurisdiction at judgment—was not present, so § 1447(c)’s remand command should not be read to mandate a post-judgment do-over where the defect has been cured. Treating the interlocutory dismissal as “infecting” the entire case even after final judgment would elevate a procedural removal error into a remedy that undermines procedural fairness and imposes substantial, unnecessary costs on litigants and courts, inviting strategic post-judgment relitigation in state court. Consistent with Newman-Green, Inc. v. Alfonzo-Larrain, 490 U.S. 826 (1989), appellate courts may preserve final judgments between diverse parties rather than reflexively vacate when jurisdiction is proper at the end of the case.
